analysis.title: Three Forces Carrying Biotech into 2027
key_insights: Franklin Equity's biotech managers say the industry enters 2027 in a stronger position than in several years, based on meetings with management teams in the US, Asia and elsewhere. Volatility in biotech equities has continued.

The US midterm elections and the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks added market uncertainty, but the authors say neither changed what biotech companies are reporting or the fundamental developments behind their outlook.

Force 1, AI: companies use AI to decide which lab experiments to run, so scientists test fewer candidate molecules before finding the right one, and to draft regulatory documentation faster, with human review.
AI may generate more lab work rather than less. Idea generation gets faster, so the bottleneck moves to real-world testing, which means more experiments and more drug programs moving forward.

AI-designed molecules have reached late-stage trials but none is approved. For platforms that use AI to identify new disease targets, initial human validation could come within two to three years. Whether these medicines work in patients is still untested.

Force 2, China: Chinese biotechs are producing more sophisticated science and moving candidates into human trials faster than many Western peers. China announced a five-year plan in September to build on that position.

The authors see China as more opportunity than threat for the sector. Large pharma companies facing patent expirations are licensing China-originated assets to refill pipelines, which also validates the underlying science.
Western laboratory suppliers say China spending is recovering strongly, ahead of some expectations, but is still below its 2021-2022 peak.

Several companies are withholding early-stage pipeline detail because of competition from China. The authors argue pipeline slides are now a less reliable guide, and that companies with a proven discovery record may carry upside the market has not priced.

Force 3, fundamentals: lab suppliers' order books show demand picking up, led by drug R&D rather than manufacturing. One large supplier has orders ahead of sales and another raised its outlook on a stronger backlog.

Science and access are advancing: cell therapies developed for cancer are showing promise in lupus and other autoimmune diseases, a bladder-cancer treatment that could let some patients avoid bladder removal is approaching regulatory filing, and GLP-1 drugs are reaching lower-income Americans through Medicaid.
Biopharma M&A dollar value in 2026 has already passed the full-year 2025 total. Pace slowed in September and October ahead of the midterms. Deal count YTD 2026 matches 2025.
M&A drivers: large pharma faces significant patent expirations and looks to biotech for pipeline, and mid-sized biotechs with cash from product launches have broadened the buyer base.

Drug pricing is the main risk: US government programs are expected to pay less for some medicines and Germany is debating health spending cuts. Companies describe the impact as manageable, and many forecasts exclude uncertain overseas revenue, so the authors see a low bar where 'less bad' news lifts estimates.

Conclusion: the authors think share prices in a number of cases do not fully reflect improving fundamentals, and favor fundamental stock-pickers who look beyond disclosed pipelines. They note setbacks will occur.

sector_views.rationale: Fundamentals (R&D spending, new medicines, M&A) are improving faster than sentiment, and expectations on drug pricing already look cautious, so authors see selective upside.

earnings_insights: Laboratory suppliers cited by the authors report improving orders: one large supplier has orders running ahead of sales and another raised its outlook on a stronger backlog. Company names, figures and basis are not given.
risk_factors: Drug pricing: lower US government program payments for some medicines and possible German health spending cuts.
Public financing for biotech remains selective and budgets are still scrutinized.
Policy, financing conditions and valuations remain important influences on biotech.
AI-designed drugs are unproven in patients and none is approved.
Competition from China raises the bar for Western companies and is reducing disclosure of early-stage pipelines.
Small biotechs face survival risk from a single failed trial, and the authors say not every company will execute well.
charts_described: Exhibit 1: Benchling and Statista survey of 104 biotech and pharma companies shows 81% use AI in scientific use cases and 92% in non-scientific use cases.
Exhibit 2: Chinese biopharma out-licensing deal value rose from $24.1B in 2022 to $25.5B in 2023, $51.8B in 2024 and $105.1B in 2025.

Exhibit 3: Biotech acquisitions with at least $50M in guaranteed proceeds, 2018 to YTD 2026 as of 19 October 2026. The number of acquisitions has matched 2025 while total dollar value has exceeded it.
vol_and_positioning: Biotech equities have had continued periods of volatility in 2026. The authors say 2026's volatility shows how quickly sentiment can change.
Expectations look cautious: many forecasts exclude uncertain overseas drug revenue, which the authors say sets a low bar for estimate revisions.
geopolitical: China's government announced a five-year plan in September to build on its biotech position.
US midterm elections slowed biopharma M&A in September and October as buyers became more selective, and the authors say the election outcome removes one source of uncertainty.
Germany is debating health spending cuts, and US government programs are expected to pay less for some medicines.

tension_points.bull_case: R&D spending, new medicines and M&A are improving, expectations on drug pricing are cautious, and 'less bad' news would lift estimates.
tension_points.bear_case: Budgets are still scrutinized, public financing is selective and drug pricing concerns persist, with US programs expected to pay less for some medicines and Germany debating spending cuts.

theme_stances.key_argument: Research spending, new medicines and deal-making are picking up faster than sentiment, and share prices in a number of cases do not fully reflect it.
theme_stances.evidence: fundamentals are improving faster than the market outlook

theme_stances.key_argument: China is more opportunity than threat as pharma licenses China-originated assets to refill pipelines.
